analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from forcing workers and consumers into private arbitration for job, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes.
analysis.headline: The FAIR Act, which would ban forced arbitration of worker, consumer, and civil rights disputes, drew 102 House cosponsors and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAIR Act would amend federal arbitration law so that companies cannot make people sign away their day in court before a dispute exists. It would invalidate forced arbitration clauses and class-action waivers covering employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes, while leaving voluntary arbitration after a dispute arises untouched. Companies would have to let workers and consumers take those cases to court or join class actions instead of being shunted into a private arbitration system chosen by the company.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, workers and consumers who currently sign away their right to sue as a condition of a job, a phone plan, a credit card, or an online account would keep their access to the courts. That includes people with discrimination or harassment claims, employees misclassified as independent contractors, and consumers in small-dollar disputes that only make sense as a class action. Voluntary post-dispute arbitration would remain available.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and consumers facing forced arbitration

how_it_helps.text: It makes predispute arbitration agreements unenforceable for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes, so companies could not use a job or loan contract to force cases into a private arbitration system they largely control.

It also voids predispute class-action waivers, restoring the right of workers and consumers to pool together in a joint or class action, which is often the only practical way to challenge small-dollar harms.
It leaves the decision about whether the ban applies to a court, not an arbitrator, and preserves arbitration that is agreed to voluntarily after a dispute has actually arisen.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that rely on forced arbitration and class-action waivers — banks, employers, tech platforms, telecoms, and other consumer-facing businesses — would lose a legal shield that keeps most disputes out of court and out of class actions. Arbitration providers would lose a large share of their business. Some cost of litigation could be passed on in prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill is broad: it voids predispute arbitration not just for wage and consumer disputes but also for antitrust and civil rights cases, which critics would say goes further than needed to fix the most obvious abuses.

Businesses would lose arbitration as a lower-cost alternative to litigation for the covered disputes, and some of the cost of expanded court litigation could show up in prices or in more drawn-out legal fights for both sides.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the benefit is real: without forced arbitration, consumers and workers can take disputes to court and join class actions, which is often the only practical way to challenge small-dollar harms. The cost is that companies lose a faster, cheaper dispute channel and may face more litigation, and some of that cost could be passed through. Supporters say those costs are small compared with restoring accountability; the main design objection is the bill's breadth, since it covers antitrust and civil rights cases, not just employment and consumer contracts.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee, where the bill was sent in April 2023, never acted on it, so it sat for the rest of the 118th Congress without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Hank Johnson introduced the FAIR Act in the House on April 27, 2023, and it was referred to the Judiciary Committee.
102 of 216 House Democrats signed on as cosponsors.
The last recorded action is the referral; no hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate companion action appears in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that rely on forced arbitration to keep employment and consumer disputes out of court keep that power for at least another Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that force customers and workers into arbitration

for.name: Rep. Hank Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAIR Act on April 27, 2023 and made introductory remarks.

for.name: 102 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill after referral, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House agenda in the 118th Congress and never brought the bill to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 102 cosponsors were House Democrats, and with Republicans holding the House majority, no Republican support moved the bill through a GOP-controlled Judiciary Committee.

industries.note: The consumer and employment arbitration industry would lose the large volume of cases that companies currently require into private arbitration, since those disputes could go to court instead.

industries.industry: Financial services, telecom, and consumer-facing businesses
industries.note: Companies that use forced arbitration and class-action waivers to keep customer and worker complaints out of court and out of class actions would face class litigation instead, changing their legal exposure.
